items.title: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wants to build an aluminum rolling mill in Canada
items.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says new federal investments announced Friday are a first step toward reducing the Canadian aluminum sector’s dependence on the United States.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Industry Minister Mélanie Joly speaks during Question Period in Ottawa on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says new federal investments announced Friday are a first step toward reducing the Canadian aluminum sector’s dependence on the United States.
items.body:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says new federal investments announced Friday are a first step toward reducing the Canadian aluminum sector’s dependence on the United States.

Joly, who is also the minister responsible for economic development in Quebec, made the comments in La Baie, Que., where she announced more than $193 million in federal funding for projects at four Rio Tinto facilities in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region and at the Alouette aluminum smelter in Sept-Îles, Que.

“The aluminum industry is much more than an economic driver. It is also a strategic industry for our country and for Canadian sovereignty,” the minister said in her speech.

Citing the economic upheaval caused by tariffs and the unpredictability of the American government, Joly said that “in this new context, we must be able to produce more of what our economy needs right here in Canada.”

She also said the funding is a first step toward strengthening the Canadian aluminum supply chain.

Joly pointed out that the price of aluminum products are inflated first by tariffs when they enter the United States and a second time when that aluminum returns to Canada.

The United States imposes a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian aluminum, and since Sept. 8, Canada has imposed a 50 per cent tariff on processed aluminum from the United States, resulting in a total surcharge of 100 per cent.

The Canadian tariff imposed in March 2025 was 25 per cent before Sept. 8.

Joly stressed that the government sees aluminum as a strategic sector for the Canadian economy and that she sees the importance of building rolling mills in Canada.

“It’s not normal that most of our aluminum is processed in the United States and then comes back at a higher cost to our companies,” she said.

She said several sectors — including agri-food, beverages, and aerospace — need more processed aluminum and have rolling mill projects of their own.

“We want to be able to produce our aluminum cans here at home; we want to be able to produce our aircraft and aerospace parts here at home; and we also want to attract key investments in aluminum processing for our defence sector,” Joly said.

On top of providing financial support to producers, she said the government also wants to work with entrepreneurs interested in developing these rolling mills and take on equity stakes.

Ottawa also wants “to be able to offer procurement contracts, certainly defence-related ones, for key components in the aerospace sector, precisely to create a business model that makes sense for a rolling mill,” Joly stated.

“Economic sovereignty isn’t something you proclaim, it’s something you build.”

Canada has nine primary aluminum smelters, eight of which are located in Quebec. The other is in British Columbia.

items.title: ‘Something to worry about’: Parliamentary budget officer concerned about Carney government’s debt levels ahead of budget
items.description: Canada’s parliamentary budget officer is raising concerns over Canada’s debt levels, with the federal government set to table its budget in a little over a week.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s parliamentary budget officer is raising concerns over Canada’s debt levels, with the federal government set to table its budget in a little over a week.
items.body:
Canada’s parliamentary budget officer is raising concerns over Canada’s debt levels, with the federal government set to table its budget in a little over a week.

The PBO released her latest economic forecast on Tuesday, which is projecting slower growth in the country’s real GDP forecast, and laying the blame at the feet of the U.S. tariff war on Canada. The outlook also spells trouble for the federal government’s debt, and the cost of servicing that debt, projecting a growing debt-to-GDP ratio in the coming years.

Declining deficit-to-GDP ratio is one of the federal government’s fiscal anchors. But, according to PBO Annette Ryan, the charges to service the debt is “the fastest-growing piece of government spending right now.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“It sounds like a strong word to say ‘anchor,’ that spending is going to be held in check, but keep in mind … the government has a very, very expansionary plan,” Ryan told CTV Question Period host Vassy Kapelos in an interview airing Sunday, when asked what that means for the fiscal health of the government’s finances.

Ryan also pointed to the Liberals’ plans for pipelines and high-speed rail as examples of large ticket items.

“And they are both spending a lot and borrowing a lot,” she said. “So, I wanted to put that in play, because the anchors are really more like traffic lights instead of an anchor that holds down spending.”

The federal government classifies its spending in two ways: capital and operational. Last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government is on track to balance its operating budget by 2027-28, one year earlier than he first promised.

Ryan, however, projects the federal government will miss that target by a year.

Expanding on the metaphor of traffic lights rather than anchors, Ryan said it appears the federal government is comfortable greenlighting capital spending, whereas operational spending, rather than getting a red light, is more of a yellow.

“Revenues are up strongly,” Ryan told Kapelos. “Operating spending is up strongly as well.”

“So that anchor, we did an assessment in our report, and essentially said that that provides limited fiscal discipline, (by) not stopping spending,” she continued.

Referencing the deficit as a share of GDP, Ryan said government borrowing over the next five years is set to go up — and be “back ended” — so while the deficit is “a bit improved” this year, it’ll be worse by the end of five years.

Asked by Kapelos whether she’s worried about that, Ryan said she “wanted to flag to parliamentarians that it’s something to worry about for sure.”

“It goes to defence spending, so you’re getting an asset associated with that cash spending, that’ll enter the books as it’s essentially depreciated,” she said. “But a lot of that money, a $400-billion difference, will be going to Crown corporations, loans, special funds that are just a step removed from parliamentary oversight.”

“To the extent that the government comes forward with transparency and accountability, then I think that that takes down that worry level,” she added. “But there are definitely new risks when you move in that direction.”

Ryan said taking all those things into account, the first thing she’ll be looking for in the federal budget on Nov. 5 is the deficit, specifically how it will look in the middle term.

You can watch Parliamentary Budget Office Annette Ryan’s full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha

items.title: Trump to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods. Here’s what we know
items.description: The White House has made another wide-ranging shuffle to its tariff regime on Canadian goods. The announcements came after one GOP senator said she secured tariff exemptions to help her state.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump, plywood and seaweed are shown in a combination photo. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein/THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jeff McIntosh/Chad Hipolito)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The White House has made another wide-ranging shuffle to its tariff regime on Canadian goods. The announcements came after one GOP senator said she secured tariff exemptions to help her state.
items.body:
The White House has made another wide-ranging shuffle to its tariff regime on Canadian goods.

Among those products: Seaweed, packing boxes and some plywood sheets are out. Cocoa powder, vinyl flooring and shampoos are in.

A full list of goods now facing 50 per cent tariffs is available here. The changes will take effect at the end of the month.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office said the government will assess the latest tariff measures and that “Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship” with the U.S.

“As always, our focus remains clear: building a stronger, more competitive, and more resilient economy for workers, businesses, farmers and all Canadians” the statement said.

Earlier on Friday, Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she has secured tariff exemptions on a variety of Canadian products to bolster domestic agriculture.

“I am pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions (for) products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers,” she wrote on X Friday.

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”

Collins requested tariff relief during discussions with U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer, Treasury Secretary Howard Lutnick – both of whom have been involved in negotiations with Canada – and senior Trump administration officials, she said.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

During those conversations, she advocated for a broader trade agreement with Canada, “our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”

Collins is in the midst of a re-election campaign against Democratic candidate Troy Jackson.

Canada-U.S. deal is close: Trump

The news came hours after U.S. President Donald Trump said a trade deal with Canada is nearing.

Asked about progress toward a deal with Mexico, Trump said during a scrum with reporters in Washington that his administration is “very close” to a “very good” deal.

“The same thing with Canada. Canada’s working very hard to make a deal with us. And I hate to say this, but we have all the cards,” he said.

Progress on the Canada-U.S. trade file has been relatively opaque since talks fell apart in August. Sources told CTV News this week that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s advisory committee on U.S. economic relations convened its first meeting in over a month and a half on Thursday.

CTV News also confirmed that LeBlanc is in Ottawa on Friday, when he was expected to attend an infrastructure-related event in his New Brunswick riding.

‘All about politics?’

From Washington, CTV News political analyst Eric Ham said the exemptions are “all about politics.”

“The internal polling data must show that Susan Collins is in deep, deep trouble,” he said. “What we’re seeing here is, clearly, Republicans are sounding the alarm about what is happening just 10 days out from the election.

“And right now, we see that those tariffs have been causing tremendous angst for American voters.”

Ham said his assessment of this and other recent comments from Trump, are that it’s the president “to do his level best to give his candidates a lifeline as voters are heading to the polls.”

Meanwhile, international trade lawyer Barry Appleton said Washington’s overall tariff policy remains the same.

“Washington didn’t lower the tariff wall ... they kind of moved some bricks around,” he said in an interview with CTV News Channel Friday.

“Tariffs have a price ceiling, and Maine has now found out what that ceiling was.”

Appleton said Friday’s decision indicates that affordability has taken its toll. He called Collins “a very good friend” to Canada, but added that, “for a U.S. senator to be able to get re-elected … they have to lower tariffs.”

Robert Glasgow, an international trade lawyer with KPMG Law, said the move to add and drop tariffs is mostly about the midterm U.S. elections, noting that he believes Trump received “significant pressure” from Collins to modify the list.

“I think early on, there were announcements – including by Senator Collins – that she got in items removed,” he said in an interview with CTV News Channel Friday. “But it’s very important to note that the White House also came out quickly with a list of items, ranging from cocoa powder to carpets that are now on the list in their place,” Glasgow added.

Glasgow said the number of items going on the list is greater than the number going off it. He said a broader trade deal is unlikely within the next few weeks, and many of the tariffed items will “likely have a relatively small impact in the immediate term.”

Carney quips ‘we could sign it this afternoon’

During an overnight press conference in Istanbul, hours before Trump’s comments, Carney said Canada was “continuing to engage with the U.S. government.”

“We continue to be ready to sit down in good faith to negotiate a trade deal that is in both of our interests. Of course, we’re looking for the interests of Canadians, we don’t care about the timing of that,” he said.

“We could sign it [a deal] this afternoon if the U.S. were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we would do that,” the prime minister told reporters.

Pressed on how much the timing matters, Carney said Canada would “drop everything” if the Americans were ready to negotiate in good faith, but the chance of that happening before the midterms is “up to the United States, they’re a little hard to predict.”

The two men spoke on Wednesday “for quite some time,” according to the prime minister. Sources have indicated to CTV News that Canadian officials haven’t ruled out the possibility of a snap trade deal before next month’s midterm elections in the U.S., but hope remains faint.

Meanwhile, Washington’s envoy in Ottawa has accused senior Canadian leadership of political interference ahead of those elections. The claims surround various officials’ activities south of the border. Among those named was Industry Minister Melanie Joly, who on Thursday refuted the claims.

She made the remark after warning a U.S. company to reverse course on a plan to lay off 500 Ontario steel workers. Stelco, in Hamilton, is owned by an Ohio-based company called Cleveland-Cliffs. Its CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, has previously publicly supported Trump’s tariff policy.

In March 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump hit Canada’s steel and aluminum sector with 25 per cent tariffs, then in June of that year, his administration increased those tariffs to 50 per cent. It’s just one sector among many affected by Trump’s expansive tariff regime.

Canada has put counter-tariffs covering $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S., with an emphasis on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

With files from CTV News Ottawa Bureau Correspondent Jeremie Charron and CTV News’ Kayla Thompson, Archie Niari and Christl Dabu

items.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training after security overhaul, discloses flaw in widely used software
items.description: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jeff Chiu / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software.
items.body:
OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defences.

The disclosure comes amid concerns over the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software flaws, including in the guardrails meant to contain them.

OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models used a configuration error to gain limited internet access in September. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its defences.

To test them, OpenAI had teams of AI agents try to break out of their restricted environments. It said the agents found previously unknown flaws, which it had fixed, and training resumed on Oct. 1.

During that exercise, the ChatGPT maker found a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool.

The company said attackers could exploit the flaw by sending malicious data that lets them run their own code on affected systems, including those using popular web software such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy.

OpenAI said the root cause was fixed in Brotli’s source code in February, before it was known to create a security vulnerability, but no new version was released at the time.

Brotli has since released updated versions and published a public record of the flaw after OpenAI disclosed it.

Separately on Thursday, AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year.

OpenAI told the safety organizations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes.

OpenAI has been conducting a broad review of its AI models’ activity since the Hugging Face incident in July, and has informed more than 100 organizations about incidents of unauthorized activity tied to its AI agents.

(Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru, Chris Thomas in Mexico City; Editing by Pooja Desai and Stephen Coates)

items._ogDesc: BP announced a deal on Friday that provides Louisiana an accelerated, lump-sum US$350 million payment to resolve claims over the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.
items.body:
BP announced a deal on Friday that provides Louisiana an accelerated, lump-sum US$350 million payment to resolve claims over the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and that also settles long-running coastal damage litigation by local parishes.

BP agreed in 2015 to pay up to US$18.7 billion to the federal government and five states to resolve claims arising out of the oil spill. That money includes US$4.9 billion payable over 18 years to settle economic and other claims by the states.

While Louisiana had been owed US$373 million over the next seven years, the state will now receive a single US$350 million payment.

BP said remaining coastal zone lawsuits by Louisiana parishes will be resolved. It did not provide further details.

“We have now disposed of claims and settled with all but one of the major defendants in these coastal cases,” Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, said in a statement distributed by BP.

(Reporting by Ankita Bora in Bengaluru and Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Joyjeet Das)

items.description: Toyota is recalling 24,454 Sienna Hybrid minivans in Canada from model years 2022 to 2026 because second-row seatbacks could move in a crash. Owners are advised not to use the second-row seats to transport passengers until dealers update the restraint system software.

items._ogDesc: Toyota is recalling 24,454 Sienna Hybrid minivans in Canada from model years 2022 to 2026 because second-row seatbacks could move in a crash. Owners are advised not to use the second-row seats to transport passengers until dealers update the restraint system software.
items.body:
Toyota is recalling more than 24,000 Sienna Hybrid minivans in Canada because a problem with the second-row seat recliners could increase the risk of injury in a crash.

The recall affects vehicles from model years 2022 to 2026, according to a notice published by Transport Canada on Oct. 20 and updated Oct. 23.

The notice says the mechanisms that lock the second-row seat recliners in position may disengage under certain conditions when a seatbelt pretensioner activates.

As a result, the seatbacks could move during a crash, potentially increasing the risk of injury to occupants.

Toyota advises owners not to use the second-row seats to

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

transport passengers until the recall repairs have been completed.

The automaker will notify affected owners by mail and instruct them to take their vehicles to a dealership. Dealers will update the software in the supplemental restraint system (SRS) electronic control unit, which controls the seatbelt pretensioners.

Owners can check whether their vehicle is affected by entering their vehicle identification number (VIN) on Toyota Canada’s recall lookup page⁠ or contact Toyota at 1-888-869-6828 for more information.

items.title: Stock markets in Canada and the U.S. slide on AI fears, higher oil prices
items.description: Canada’s main stock index finished in negative territory as North American markets felt pressure from higher oil prices and concerns about the AI trade.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s main stock index finished in negative territory as North American markets felt pressure from higher oil prices and concerns about the AI trade.
items.body:
TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index finished the week in negative territory as North American markets felt pressure from higher oil prices and concerns about the AI trade.

“The main setbacks for the markets, TSX and North America in general, came really in two forms,” said Allan Small, senior investment adviser at iA Private Wealth. 

“One is this idea of a technology pullback ... and this idea that perhaps companies are spending too much on AI and not getting the return on their investment for the capital that they are putting out, and that is a big fear.” 

The S&P/TSX composite index was down 185.27 points at 35,788.18.    

In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 652.82 points at 52,215.16. The S&P 500 index was down 39.75 points at 7,623.68, while the Nasdaq composite was down 53.52 points at 25,955.34.

  • Real-time TSX market updates here

Small said another risk facing the tech sector is that “AI can’t just go to the moon forever.”

“At some point, memory chips, the production of them would have to slow because the market would have enough memory chips.”

But falling AI stock prices could also mark a buying opportunity for some investors. 

“There are a lot of names that are a lot cheaper than they were just a little while ago, although I will say that for tech, the highs were probably back at the beginning of the summer,” Small said. 

He said the second major issue that markets grappled with this week was higher energy prices from the war in the Middle East and fears of potential escalation. 

“We’re seeing oil prices move higher on this idea ... that after the U.S. midterms, the war could ramp up once again. We have not seen really any missiles flying for a while now, but President Trump made some comments recently which has led people to believe that there could be renewed hostilities in the Middle East,” he said. 

The December crude oil contract was up US$3.80 at US$103.27 per barrel.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

Higher energy prices are also playing a crucial role in investor expectations that the Bank of Canada will hike its key lending rate next week. Financial market odds for a hike next Wednesday stood at nearly 78 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.    

“My view on that is I think it would be foolish for the Bank of Canada to hike interest rates. I think it would be foolish for the Bank of Canada to focus on inflation when we have an economy that is really not doing a heck of a lot,” Small said, adding that growth has been muted. 

The U.S. Federal Reserve is also scheduled to make an interest rate announcement on Wednesday. 

“The odds of a hike in the U.S. are down quite substantially ... so it doesn’t look like they’re going to go. The odds are now that if they move, they’ll move in December,” Small said. 

The Canadian dollar traded for 71.46 cents US compared with 71.32 cents US on Thursday.  

The December gold contract was down US$52.50 at US$4,007.90 an ounce.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Wall Street loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
items.description: Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market.

items._ogDesc: Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower Friday as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent, adding to its decline from a day before. The index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain.

Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the market, where nearly three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.1 per cent to settle at US$116.72. It has surged from less than US$97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since June 2022.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher.

The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive.

“Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent.

American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade.

JPMorgan Chase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent.

While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent.

European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit.

Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late Thursday.

Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation.

Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world’s oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 39.75 points to 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 652.82 points to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq gave up 53.52 points to close at 25,955.34.

Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

items.title: How Canadian publishers are pushing back against AI
items.description: In the absence of surefire technology to determine whether something was written by artificial intelligence, some Canadian publishers say they have to rely on something nearly as thorny: trust.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Books line shelves at the North York Central Library in Toronto on Friday, Feb. 23, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chris Young]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Chris Young</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: In the absence of surefire technology to determine whether something was written by artificial intelligence, some Canadian publishers say they have to rely on something nearly as thorny: trust.
items.body:
TORONTO — In the absence of surefire technology to determine whether something was written by artificial intelligence, some Canadian publishers say they have to rely on something nearly as thorny: trust.

Alana Wilcox, the editorial director of Coach House Books, wrote in an email that the company asks writers to be upfront about whether their work contains material generated by AI.

She said the existing tools to discern the use of AI have proven unreliable and problematic.

“As AI becomes more sophisticated, we don’t imagine the existing tools will become more reliable — it will become more and more difficult to identify AI use,” she wrote.

There is renewed attention on the role of artificial intelligence in the book industry after a Quebec publisher cut ties with an author accused of using AI to write his debut novel.

Earlier this week, Montreal-based publishing house Les Éditions du Boréal said an analysis of some documents’ metadata found evidence author Thélyson Orélien used AI while writing his novel “C’était ça ou mourir” (“It was either that or dying”).

Allegations that Orélien used AI in his book first emerged on social media in September. The author denied using AI to write the book but said he had used it for research. Orélien did not respond to The Canadian Press’ request for comment following the publisher’s announcement on Wednesday.

Before the controversy, the novel had been nominated for several major French literary awards and won the Prix du Roman Fnac. It has since been removed from contention for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt. 

Les Éditions du Boréal didn’t specify which metadata showed the AI use.

And while the allegations against Orélien illustrate that trust may not always be enough, Wilcox said the Toronto-based Coach House Books doesn’t see much of an alternative.

“Our contract asks the author to affirm that their book does not contain AI-generated material. But there is no reliable way to police this: the tools that exist have proven unreliable and problematic in countless ways,” she wrote.

“Nor are we interested in supporting systems that were trained on stolen material — our books,” she added, referencing the fact that AI detection tools are, themselves, artificial intelligence.

David Caron, the co-publisher of Toronto-based ECW Press, said their author contracts include language around AI use in the warranty clause, which asks an author to guarantee specific facts about their manuscript -- including that the work is original and wholly owned by the writer.

“We have to rely on you to tell us what it is that you’ve done and what’s here in your manuscript,” Caron said. ”Our best is what we can do, but we rely on the author to tell us about the things that we don’t know.”

Lisa Quinn, president of the Association of Canadian Publishers, said “the publishing industry strongly believes that artistic creation, intellectual creation is a human-centred activity.”

But Quinn, who is also the executive director of McGill-Queen’s University Press, said AI technology is a broad descriptor and there is nuance in how assistive AI tools can be used in publishing. 

For example, she said there is a significant difference between using assistive AI technology to help in the translation of a sentence for comprehension versus using generative AI to produce a translation of a complex work.

“Those uses are radically different … where the AI is in fact a generative AI engaged in the act of writing,” she said.

Like Wilcox, Quinn said she has concerns about relying on AI-detection technology because they’re predictive models built on “truthiness rather than truth,” she said.

“A perfect answer will not be forthcoming,” Quinn said. “What you will get is a likelihood that something may or may not be the case. And that I think puts writers and publishers in a very, very difficult position.”

Quinn said the evolution of AI technology is outpacing the industry’s ability to set policies around it and there are unanswered questions about how to regulate it.

“This is where, I think, having clear policy as a publisher is helpful, but it must be built on a relationship of trust and with the human-centred principle very clearly a component of that trust.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

(Kristina Solovyova, Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Kristina Solovyova</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States under a new import agreement has set sail, the Kremlin said Friday, two weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump said he struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin despite Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
items.body:
A first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States under a new import agreement has set sail, the Kremlin said Friday, two weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump said he struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin despite Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.

“The first oil tanker has sailed off to customers, and regular supplies will continue,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said without elaborating.

The diesel deal was seen as an attempt by Trump to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

It caused alarm and dismay in Ukraine, which has pleaded with foreign countries to tighten sanctions on Moscow and deny it revenue for the invasion launched in February 2022. In the U.S., the agreement was also criticized by both Republicans and Democrats for violating American laws and drawing the country closer to Russia. The deal joins a growing list of actions in which the Republican president has sided with Putin, often at Ukraine’s expense.

Marine intelligence firm Kpler said the vessel signaled that it was headed to New York to arrive Nov. 7 and would be the first Russian diesel delivery to the United States since July 2023.

The import agreement, which Trump says foresees millions more tons of Russian diesel reaching the U.S. in the coming months, is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said earlier this week that the first shipment would amount to 40,000 tons of diesel, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency. That’s around 300,000 barrels, or about seven per cent of the roughly four million barrels of diesel the U.S. economy consumes in a single day.

Russia’s diesel production has come under strain from repeated Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries. The attacks caused fuel shortages, which now have eased. Trump last month asked Kyiv to stop the attacks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Trump’s deal “a weak decision by strong partners.”

The diesel agreement was a sudden policy reversal, coming just weeks after Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package that called for up to 100 per cent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas. He later put the measures on hold.

The development is the latest twist in the at times volatile relationship between Trump and Zelenskyy, which in recent weeks has sunk to a new low.

Starlink still isn’t back to normal despite U.S. promises, Zelenskyy says

Zelenskyy said he spoke Friday with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, after they consulted with Putin in St. Petersburg. They also spoke with the Ukrainian leader earlier this week in Norway.

Kyiv is keen to add momentum to peace efforts in a planned three-way meeting between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that may take place next month at a venue to be decided, Zelenskyy said in comments via video link to the Hudson Institute research organization in Washington.

“We need diplomacy to move forward,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine’s pressing issues are protecting its power grid from Russian attacks ahead of winter, getting more U.S.-made Patriot air-defence interceptors to counter Russia’s ballistic missiles and finding more financial support from foreign countries, Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine is still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits that are choking its drone operations, Zelenskyy said. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier this week that the satellite internet service would be fully restored within 72 hours, according to the Ukrainian leader.

Moscow airports temporarily close, and other developments

Meanwhile, Russia’s civil aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, said Friday afternoon that all four Moscow airports -- Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky -- stopped flights arriving and departing for security reasons.

At Sheremetyevo airport, passengers were told to take shelter, Russian news agency Interfax reported. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that air defences downed 21 Ukrainian drones targeting the Russian capital in the afternoon.

The airport restrictions were lifted three hours later.

In other developments, the White House announced that first lady Melania Trump brokered an upcoming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the war-ravaged Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians.

The first lady said in a news release that the situation there is “on the brink of disaster.”

Ukraine’s top negotiator involved in the humanitarian mission told The Associated Press that the local ceasefire would start Tuesday -- two days before the mission begins -- and last several days.

Also Friday, Russia and Ukraine exchanged hundreds of prisoners of war for the first time since August.

The Russian Defense Ministry said each side released 270 prisoners. Ukraine said 270 of its soldiers and civilians were freed, most of them held in captivity since 2022.

Elsewhere, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said a Russian embassy staff member has been declared persona non grata after a Russian drone violated the country’s airspace and crashed near homes.

Police said a local resident discovered a drone in the village of Chistelnita in Telenesti District, less than 100 metres (330 feet) from a home. Specialists were sent to investigate. No one was reported hurt.

“Russia’s war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk,” Sandu wrote on X. “Today, a Russian Geran attack drone violated our airspace and fell near family homes and an energy facility.”

Stephen McGrath in Leamington Spa, England, contributed.

items.title: Northern B.C. housing market holds relatively steady as local economy recovers
items.description: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items._ogDesc: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items.body:
Northern B.C.’s housing market is holding relatively steady compared with other parts of the province, supported by a recovery in the local economy over the summer, according to the BC Northern Real Estate Board (BCNREB).

The board reported 1,009 seasonally adjusted residential sales in the third quarter of 2026, down 3.1 per cent from the same period last year and 3.9 per cent below historical averages.

The average sale price across the board’s region reached $464,180, up 0.1 per cent from the previous quarter.

“In comparison to other board regions in B.C., the North most closely follows its historical average sales levels, hovering between four to eight per cent below that benchmark across the past few quarters,” the BCNREB said in a release published earlier in October.

The board said the relative stability "has corresponded with a resurgence in the local economy over the summer, with our nowcast measure of Northern economic growth now closely following its provincial counterpart after a largely contractionary 2025.”

Much of this recovery is attributable to “robust” employment growth in the North Coast and Cariboo areas, according to the BCNREB.

Prince George recorded the most sales in the region in the first nine months of the year, with 1,043 properties worth $531.4 million changing hands, a 2.1 per cent decline from the same period last year. Fort St. John followed, with 541 properties worth $244.9 million sold, down 3.6 per cent year-over-year.

“The sales-to-active listings ratio remained largely flat from the previous quarter, hovering near 18.2 per cent, keeping Northern markets near the upper threshold of balanced conditions,” the board said.

Looking ahead, the BCNREB warned that inflationary pressures and rising bond yields have pushed five-year fixed mortgage rates above five per cent, potentially limiting housing demand.

Taking into account current national economic and labour market conditions, markets were also anticipating further Bank of Canada interest rate increases in 2027, according to the report.

“Despite these headwinds, we continue to expect sales activity in the North to outperform the rest of B.C., underpinned by relatively better affordability conditions,” said the board.

The post Halifax Real Estate Prices Just Made The Second-Biggest Drop On Record appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Halifax home prices posted their second-largest monthly dollar drop on record as September new listings hit a six-year high, despite rising sales.
items.body:
Greater Halifax real estate may be running out of luck. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows a six-year high for new listings in September. Sales also rose, but couldn’t prevent the second-largest monthly price drop on record.

Halifax Home Prices Post Second-Largest Monthly Drop On Record

The price of a typical home sold through the MLS across Halifax-Dartmouth.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Greater Halifax home prices fell sharply last month. The price of a typical home dropped 3.9% (-$22.1k) to $541,700 in September, leaving prices 4.1% (-$23.4k) below last year. In dollar terms, it was the second-largest monthly drop on record, only beaten by the May 2022 plunge after rate hikes began. Prices are now 5.4% (-$31.0k) below the May 2026 record high, bringing them to their lowest level since December 2024.

Home Sales Rise But Remain Below Pre-Pandemic Volumes

Halifax-Dartmouth home sales through the MLS in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Existing home sales rose but remain tepid. A total of 434 homes sold in September, up 4% from last year but still well below pre-pandemic levels. Rising sales aren’t an obvious driver of falling prices, but volumes remain weak—and look worse against elevated inventory.

Halifax New Listings Hit A Six-Year High For September

Halifax-Dartmouth new listings of homes for sale in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

September isn’t traditionally a big month for sellers, but last month was an exception. CREA reported 727 new listings in September, up 1.4% from last year. That increase looks modest next to sales growth, but new listings have climbed for four years straight. Last month saw the highest September volume since 2020.

Halifax-Dartmouth has largely resisted the price declines dragging down the national benchmark. However, that resilience was based on a relatively small pool of buyers. Thin sales leave prices vulnerable when those buyers pull back or when sellers face more competition. With listings rising and prices falling sharply, the market may now be testing where buyers are willing to step in.

items.title: B.C. billionaire's real estate firms allege 'pattern of misconduct' by CRA in tax row
items.description: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items._ogDesc: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items.body:
Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.

Five companies within Hui's real estate development group are targeted in the audit by the CRA, including Adex Securities, One West Holdings, a B.C. numbered company and two Luxembourg-based shell companies.

The companies filed an application in Federal Court this month, claiming the government has wrongfully moved to collect on tax debts totalling more than $200 million, most of which is accrued interest.

The application says the group is involved in capital-intensive real estate projects in Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary and the audit, initiated in 2013, focused on transactions that relied on Canada's tax treaty with Luxembourg.

The companies say in the application that they've received tax debt assessments this year, with Adex owing $45 million and interest of more than $65 million, while the two Luxembourg based companies owe together more than $92 million and $127 million in interest.

One of the companies' lawyers said in a statement that the total debt being sought by the CRA is approximately $219 million, due to "overlapping liabilities" between the entities.

The companies want the court to stop the government from collecting on the debts until a related case filed earlier this year is concluded, while objecting to the CRA wanting $115 million security payment from Adex.

Requiring a payment that large and not allowing the company to defer will cause the real estate group to "lose significant capital that is currently being used to fund active development projects."

The application is one of at least three filed in Federal Court this year related to the dispute, where they claim that being forced to pay will cause "irreparable harm" and that no advance notice from the CRA means that they "could not have reasonably planned for a debt … of this magnitude."

The companies claim the revenue agency has exhibited a "pattern of misconduct," alleging its officers acted outside established policies and procedures and "without regard to the impact of their actions on taxpayer businesses."

Lawyers for the companies were not immediately available for comment, but Justin Kutyan with KPMG Law in Toronto told The Canadian Press earlier this year that the transactions in the case were similar to a tax structure upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2021.

The court ruled 6-3 in favour of Alta Energy Luxembourg, which had claimed a tax exemption on a capital gain of more than $380 million under Canada's treaty with Luxembourg, described in the decision as being "well known as an international tax haven."

The court found in Alta's favour, ruling that Canadian tax authorities couldn't use anti-tax avoidance rules to "judicially amend or renegotiate a treaty."

The dissenting justices in the case, however, said "the federal government did not deliberately set out to create the conditions for unlimited tax avoidance by means of schemes" used by the company.

The dissenters wrote that "the court should not legitimize such blatantly abusive tax avoidance based on the view that Canada should have negotiated different treaty terms."

The CRA said it did not have a spokesperson available for an interview to comment on tax treaty abuse.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics
items.description:
Oxford Economics expects Canadian home prices to fall further as rising mortgage rates, weak hiring, and stretched valuations weigh on demand.

The post Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Oxford Economics expects Canadian home prices to fall further as rising mortgage rates, weak hiring, and stretched valuations weigh on demand.
items.body:
Canadian real estate is already in its largest correction on record by some measures, but it may get worse. A new Oxford Economics report forecasts further declines in home prices and sales as rising interest rates hit an already weak market. High energy prices, economic uncertainty, and stretched valuations are expected to add further downward pressure.

Canadian Home Prices And Sales Expected To Fall Further

Despite the severe correction in home prices, the firm sees them moving lower for at least a few months. “We expect home sales volumes and prices to slide this fall and into early next year as mortgage rates rise,” explains Tony Stillo, director of Canada economics at Oxford Economics.

He notes that home prices remain elevated relative to incomes, presenting further risk for homebuilders. Rising expectations of rate hikes add to that risk.

Bank of Canada Rate Hikes Expected Soon

The firm expects two rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of this year, the first within days. Next week they see a 25 basis point (bp) hike at the central bank’s October 28th meeting, and another in early December. Next week’s hike may be delayed by the recent weak employment data, according to Stillo. But he still sees a 50 bp increase by January, bringing the overnight rate to 2.75%, their estimate of neutral, where monetary policy neither stimulates nor throttles economic activity.

As economists are increasingly noting, the driver of rate hikes here isn’t an overheated economy. Weak economic and employment data reinforces that this isn’t an economy firing on all cylinders, but one that would struggle with rate hikes. However, Stillo explains the catalyst fueling rate hike expectations is energy prices.

Brent crude is forecast to remain above US$100 per barrel for six months, he notes. By their calculations, this is expected to push headline inflation into the mid-3% range in late 2026 and early 2027. Bond yields have already begun to reflect expectations of upward pressure.

“A rapid rise in bond yields will continue to push borrowing costs higher throughout the economy, weighing on interest-sensitive sectors like housing and spending on consumer durables,” warns Stillo.

Weak Hiring and a Shrinking Population Add To Housing Pressure

Higher interest rates won’t be the only factor working against housing activity in the near-term. “A weak job market weighed down by the ongoing trade war with the US, squeezed household incomes from high fuel prices, and a shrinking population will hurt housing demand,” explains Stillo.

He cites the 68,000 jobs lost in September—roughly 110,000 lost over the past two job reports—as evidence that hiring will remain weak over the short-term. A perfect storm of higher fuel costs squeezing disposable income, tariffs, and trade uncertainty is weighing on businesses.

Canada’s population declines are a less certain factor. Stillo expects the population to decline if policymakers maintain their goal of shrinking the share of non-permanent residents (NPRs) to 5% of the population by the end of 2027. The recent upward revisions suggest a much sharper decline would be needed to meet that goal. Oxford is awaiting Ottawa’s immigration update before revising its demographic forecast.

As for weaker households, they face a sticky situation. Higher rates will squeeze spending power, but so would higher energy prices and elevated inflation. “Elevated debt will continue to constrain spending by Canadian households and make them vulnerable to job losses, higher interest rates, and a resurgence in oil prices,” warns Stillo.

Oxford doesn’t see the downturn lasting forever—it only feels that way. The firm expects a housing recovery to start in the second half of 2027 through 2028, just a little over a half-decade since the correction began. Before then, rising borrowing costs and weak demand point to a near-term slump. However, with prices still stretched relative to incomes, Oxford warns the correction could prove deeper or longer than its baseline forecast.

items.title: Canadians’ aversion to AI slop has steered this mortgage broker toward finding the real
items.description: Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media
items.content: <p>Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639283724664853667.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media
items.body:
Artificial intelligence has been a gamechanger for the mortgage industry – but somewhat paradoxically, the rise of AI solutions is pushing plenty of mortgage brokers to find ways to amplify the human touch and focus on the value they can provide separate from ChatGPT and Claude.

For Sherry Corbitt (pictured top), a mortgage broker with Mortgage Architects in Ontario’s Durham region, that’s translated into building a social media presence on the principle that authenticity wins.

Short-form video content has become an increasingly prominent part of her marketing strategy, Corbitt told Canadian Mortgage Professional, in an approach that’s been influenced by the growing aversion of many Canadians to AI-generated slop.

Younger generations, Corbitt’s assistant told her, are not into watching videos created by AI. “They just want authentic,” Corbitt said. “They want the ums and ahs. They want somebody to just do quick, genuine stuff.”

She also works on a significant volume of reverse mortgages, a product that naturally skews toward older, Facebook-active clients, and has noticed those generations are equally resistant to AI content – for a good reason.

“They’re scared of what’s fake,” Corbitt said. “So if they want to deal with you, then you have to be authentic and do your own videos.”

A recent CIRA (Canadian Internet Registration Authority) survey revealed that over half (53%) of Canadians encountered fake content generated by AI in the past year, up from 34% in 2025 and 20% in 2024.

And a Harris Poll Canada poll found that nearly nine in 10 Canadians are concerned about deceptive online content generated by AI, while a Roku Video-on-Demand Evolution study found that four out of five Canadians believe the use of AI in advertising should be labelled.

Industry pushes back on AI-generated advice

Mortgage industry members have also flagged the potential risks posed by AI mortgage misinformation for potential homebuyers.

Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) founder and chief executive Joe White told CMP that AI “has a wonderful ability to give you an answer that sounds incredibly confident, but in many cases it’s the fine details that it gets wrong because it’s trained on everything out there on the internet – accurate information as well as inaccurate information.”

Other industry executives, including broker Angela Calla, say they’ve utilized AI for back-office workflow, but avoid it entirely for client conversations.

“We use it as a personal business resource to refine communication, strengthen our standard operating procedures, and improve efficiency,” Calla told CMP. “We don’t use AI to communicate directly with clients.”

How to jump on the authentic-content train

There’s no magic number for daily video output – Corbitt targets multiple a day, although she said each video typically focuses on addressing only one person, covering one topic, and answering one question.

That’s a formula she says creates a near-unlimited supply of material, as well as removing the production pressure that puts many brokers off starting.

Aside from knowing how to record and upload videos to social media platforms, Corbitt highlighted that the approach doesn’t require a huge amount of digital know-how. “I’m not tech savvy at all,” she said. “So being able to use just a few easy programs where you can do your subtext and things like that – it’s going really well. I’m enjoying it.”

New video content has helped Corbitt’s authenticity shine through, she said, as well as increasing brand awareness among first-time buyers and the cohort of Canadians who encounter mortgage advice while passively scrolling.

“I’m having success with my realtor partners who are dealing with first-time buyers… and the videos, I think that helps, too,” she said. “Because they’re watching the videos. So I’m not having a problem with that market.”

items.title: Markham's Nearly-Complete EverHome Condo Project Placed Under Receivership
items.description:
Another development project that’s nearing completion has become insolvent, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court — the latest in an extensive list of projects that are struggling to cross the finish line.

The project is EverHome, by Toronto-based developer The Sher Corporation, and is located at 9704 McCowan Road in Markham near the intersection with Bur Oak Avenue, just north of the Williamstown Plaza shopping centre.

For the site, The Sher Corporation is developing a mid-rise condo project with 131 units across three buildings, plus an amenity building.

For the project, The Sher Corporation — through Sher Markham Inc. and Sher Holdings Inc. — secured financing from Meridian Credit Union in July 2022 for a construction demand facility in the amount of $57,251,849.81, with interest accruing at Meridian’s Prime Rate + 1.75% per annum (with an all-in floor rate of 4.20%), plus a letters of credit facility in the amount of $1,100,590.40.

According to court filings, 103 of the 131 units — 78.6% — had been pre-sold as of July 2026. Construction was approximately 86% complete before halting in May 2026.

Construction Halts

“Construction on the Project halted in or around mid May 2026 due to reported safety concerns identified by the safety consultant, resignation of the construction manager, compounded by a funding gap and associated cost overruns,” said Meridian in an October 7 application seeking to place the project under receivership. “As at that date, the Project’s structures were substantially completed, building envelopes were near completion, and the interior works were incomplete and behind schedule.”

According to Meridian, the construction manager raised several safety issues in May 2026 to Shakeel Walji — the President and corporate director of The Sher Corporation, as well as the guarantor of the loan — including “numerous serious safety deficiencies and non-compliance items onsite, including hazards, fire safety concerns and unsafe stair access conditions, noting many of the items required immediate corrective action.”

The construction manager, Grove Inc., then terminated all work in light of the safety concerns.

A rendering of the EverHome project. (The Sher Corporation)

Eastpointe Corp. was retained as the new construction manager in July 2026, and worked with the project cost consultant, CB Ross Partners, to conduct an assessment and prepare an updated construction budget. They concluded that, as of July, the cost to complete the project was around $17.3 million, a dated number that is now expected to be larger.

According to Meridian Credit Union, The Sher Corporation has defaulted on the loan agreement on several occasions, including by failing to provide financial statements, failing to repay the loan by September 2025, failing to repay the loan by March 2026, and failing to fund cost overruns.

The Receivership

Meridian said it issued a formal demand for payment in August 2026 and gave the developer until August 17 to repay the loan. The Sher Corporation was unable to do so, and Meridian subsequently also learned that the developer had $58,650.48 in insurance premiums that were past due, which Meridian then paid in September.

Meridian says it was owed $57,731,133.87 as of September 15, 2026, with interest continuing to accrue. The lender also says that the developer has not provided a solution to address the outstanding debt and has also allowed 21 liens totalling to $11,422,954.19 to be registered against the property.

According to the lender, Walji reached out in July 2026 to explore the possibility of seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA).

According to an affidavit sworn by Walji on October 13, The Sher Corporation secured $21,150,000 in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing from Safe Harbour Global Capital to fund the potential CCAA proceeding. Walji said the financing “provides a proposed means of addressing the immediate funding shortfall that has prevented the Sher Project from being completed” and “this new new capital would preserve the value of the substantial work already completed and avoid the value destruction and additional cost that could result if construction remains incomplete or is interrupted for an extended period through a receivership proceeding.”

Meridian’s receivership application was scheduled to be heard by the court on October 14, and Walji asked for an adjournment of 30 days so they can finalize the CCAA application and DIP financing. However, the judge presiding over the case ultimately sided with Meridian.

“There is no viable CCAA option, there is real risk to the security of Meridian in waiting further and nothing but speculative chances of delay producing more than a deeper hole to dig out of,” said Judge Sean Dunphy, who added that “the very fact that Meridian prefers to take its chances in a receivership now rather than later speaks volumes as to how viable that particular DIP proposal is.”

Meridian’s receivership application was then granted, and the project is now under receivership as of October 14.

items.title: Construction costs, policy certainty top B.C. builders' priorities ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items._ogDesc: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items.body:
With the B.C. election approaching, builders across the province say they want the next government to address rising construction costs and provide greater policy consistency for the industry.

Improving the predictability of the project pipeline, transparency around how development fees are spent and communication among different levels of government are also among the priorities that building industry associations want the next government to address.

“Reducing the cost to build is felt right across the province,” said George Greenwood, CEO of the Canadian Home Builders' Association of BC (CHBA BC).

“The cost to acquire the land and then building materials, labour costs, these are all contributing to making homeownership more out of reach for average British Columbians.”

CHBA BC is calling for streamlining approval processes, reforms to the municipal infrastructure funding model and greater municipal transparency and accountability in how they calculate, collect and spend fees charged to developers.

The organization is also calling on the next government to pause potential mandatory changes to the province’s energy step codes, which set progressive energy-efficiency requirements for new construction in B.C. Greenwood argues it would add more costs to builders.

“We're just saying take a more stable approach, even putting it on a pause, let people catch their breath,” he said. “The economy is not strong right now. The housing market is not strong.”

The Vancouver Regional Construction Association (VRCA) is also urging the next government to look at ways to reduce charges imposed on developers and increase transparency on how the revenue is spent.

“The additional fees added to housing from development cost charges and other charges are not helping get housing built, not to mention all the other impacts of what's happening in the economy and interest rates,” said Jeannine Martin, president of VRCA.

“[We also want to see] more transparency on what's happening with that, what that's paying for, and how we are utilizing that to build housing.”

Chris Atchison, president of the BC Construction Association, said he also wants greater government transparency, including the reinstatement of the Major Projects Inventory reports, which was discontinued late last year.

Atchison said recent policy discussions, including a proposal to convert vacant condo units in designated growth areas into affordable homes using financing through Build Canada Homes and BC Housing, and a two per cent tax on vacant residential properties, have raised concerns about mixed policy signals to the construction industry.

“We need policy consistency and a predictable project pipeline. They're critical to housing delivery,” said Atchison.

“Because construction is a long-term industry, all of our projects can take years to plan, to finance, to approve and deliver, so businesses need confidence that the policy environment will remain stable throughout that process.”

Those who spoke with Business in Vancouver said they also hope to see better communication among different levels of government, saying there is still room for improvement, and continued investment in skilled trade training programs.

items._ogDesc: Canadian mortgage credit growth posted its weakest August since 2013. BMO warns renewed rate hikes could add pressure to borrowers.
items.body:
Canadian borrowing is losing steam just as interest rate hikes come back into focus. Bank of Canada (BoC) data shows mortgage credit posted its smallest August increase since 2013, pushing annual growth to a pace rarely seen outside housing corrections. With nearly a third of new mortgages carrying variable rates, renewed tightening could further throttle slow activity.

Canadian Mortgage Debt Growth Slows To Weakest August Since 2013

Canadian household debt: Residential mortgage credit, annual growth rate.

Source: Bank of Canada; Better Dwelling.

Residential mortgage debt advanced 0.3% (+$7.1 billion) to $2.45 trillion in August. That was unusually slow, marking the smallest August increase since 2013. Annual growth decelerated for a tenth straight month, leaving the balance only 3.8% (+$89.1 billion) higher than last year. It’s a slump that’s catching the attention of at least one Big Six economist.

“In August, household mortgage debt grew just 3.8% y/y, the slowest pace since the worst of the housing correction in 2023-24 (and before that, since the early 2000s),” explained Shelly Kaushik, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

Ontario & BC Slump, Weak New Condo Demand Slows Growth

The weak credit growth serves as a reminder that market stabilization isn’t the same as normalization. While the national market is stabilizing, it’s masking the prolonged slump in BC and Ontario. Weak demand in these regions, along with weak new condo demand in general, “has kept a lid on the recent recovery in borrowing,” according to Kaushik.

The data highlights another area the Bank of Canada (BoC) may be watching, explains Kaushik. “Canadian monthly credit aggregates, which typically fly under the radar, highlighted an ongoing slowdown in the economy’s most interest-rate-sensitive sector just as the Bank of Canada may be looking more closely at raising rates.”

Rate Hikes May Add To Mortgage Payment Stress

Bond yields are surging higher, but housing demand remains relatively weak. “Suffice it to say the housing market isn’t exactly in need of extinguishing,” says Kaushik. Variable-rate loans accounted for roughly 30% of new mortgages in Q2, according to BoC data cited by BMO, leaving those borrowers exposed to renewed rate hikes.

“Indeed, a new tightening cycle could add payment stress to variable rate mortgage holders,” she warns. Mortgage borrowing is already struggling to regain momentum. Renewed tightening could add further pressure to both the recovery and the households carrying that debt.

items.title: Could inflation fears push the Bank of Canada toward its first hike since 2023?
items.description: RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold
items.content: <p>RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282903689072151.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold
items.body:
The Bank of Canada enters its October 28 rate decision at a crossroads, with Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) economists projecting a 25-basis-point hike to the overnight rate, the first since 2023. But Frances Donald, Chief Economist at RBC in Toronto, and Nathan Janzen, Assistant Chief Economist at RBC, are not confident.

“We have very low conviction on the idea of a rate hike this soon, and it’s almost equally probable the central bank uses this meeting to tee-up a coming hike in December or January,” they wrote in an October preview.

Crucially, the RBC team is not calling for a hike on urgency grounds.

“Our expectation of a move higher from the BoC on Wednesday is not because we believe there is an urgency to hike interest rates,” Donald and Janzen wrote.

Instead, they attribute it to a shift in the Bank’s communication since its September 2 decision, which they read as signalling a preference to act preemptively against inflation rather than wait for it to materialise.

The case for patience remains strong. Canada’s labour market lost 68,300 jobs in September, its worst month of 2026, lifting the unemployment rate to 6.5%.

August gross domestic product is expected to have risen just 0.1%, below Statistics Canada’s 0.2% advance estimate.

Five-year Government of Canada bond yields have nonetheless climbed more than 40 basis points over three months, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil has averaged US$95 per barrel since the last BoC decision, 54% above year-earlier levels.

Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group says underlying inflation trends remain consistent with a wait-and-see approach, while Stéfane Marion of National Bank of Canada expects the Bank of Canada to refrain from hiking rates next week. https://t.co/7HWcvP53Lr — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

Divided views on whether a rate hike is warranted

Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge, addressing the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) National Conference in Calgary on October 18, was unambiguous.

“I don’t see rates going up anytime soon,” Laberge said.

“Governor Macklem was really, really clear that he has no tools to do anything about global inflation. He could kill the economy as much as he wants, and kill domestic inflation, but current inflation is coming from supply chain disruption and oil prices due to war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz.” 

Laberge placed his base case firmly beyond this year.

“The economy is not extremely [strong] right now. We saw the labour market numbers,” he said.

“So my hunch right now is: not before 2027. Our previous forecast was mid-2027. We may bring that forward a little, so maybe end of Q1, early Q2 2027, but I don’t see anything this year.” 

Douglas Porter, chief economist at BMO Capital Markets in Toronto, acknowledged the divided outlook.

“If anything, the threat of higher inflation has rekindled chatter of a potential rate hike in 2026,” Porter said.

“We still view that as a very long shot indeed, with the economy struggling to grow, core inflation moving closer to the 2% target, and USMCA uncertainty still clouding the outlook.” 

What the October 28 decision means for mortgage brokers

Donald and Janzen argue a 25-bps move on Wednesday would not materially alter the medium-term economic picture – their base case already assumes 100 basis points of rate increases in 2027.

For brokers, what matters more is the forward guidance that accompanies it.

“Rather than the rate hike itself, we will be monitoring for any communication that helps us understand the Bank of Canada’s expected path of interest rates ahead,” they wrote.

The RBC economists offer a broader signal that mortgage professionals should not ignore.

“Central banks do not have the same patience for inflation they might have had in the past, and are willing to act preemptively to guard against it,” Donald and Janzen wrote.

For professionals navigating Canada’s ongoing mortgage renewal wave, Laberge’s remarks underscore that portfolio risk endures regardless of Wednesday’s outcome.

“The renewal shock may be easing for some households, but the risk has not vanished,” he said.

“It has moved. It’s sitting in existing portfolios. It’s more regionally concentrated than it’s ever been, and the resale conditions are softer.” 

Adding to the complexity, the Bank will deploy Prima, its new forecasting model that places mortgage renewals at the centre of the rate-setting framework, at its October meeting for the first time.

“No model is going to solve every problem, but we are hopeful that this model will be better suited for a world with more supply shocks and in a more interconnected world,” Macklem told reporters in September.

Whether it sharpens the Bank’s read on supply-driven inflation will become clear Wednesday.
